question.text: Quantum computers are worse than classical computers at almost everything classical computers already do well — email, spreadsheets, web browsing, ordinary arithmetic. Which task is a plausible case where feeding an AI a quantum computer's OUTPUT genuinely helps, and why?
options: Any everyday AI task — a quantum computer is a faster processor across the board, so anything an AI does gets faster
Simulating quantum systems (molecules, materials) that a classical computer can't efficiently model, then training an AI on that quantum-native data
Running the AI's linear algebra (the matrix multiplications inside a neural network) through Shor/HHL-style quantum subroutines for an automatic exponential speedup
Storing a neural network's weights in superposition so one quantum chip holds exponentially more parameters than any classical chip could
question.hint: It isn't about raw speed on ordinary computing — think about what KIND of data a quantum computer can produce that a classical computer structurally struggles to.

explain.g: A quantum computer is not a faster version of your laptop — for ordinary tasks (spreadsheets, web pages, most AI training as usually done) it's actually much worse, because it's built to do one very specific weird thing: hold and evolve a genuinely quantum state. That specific thing turns out to be useful for AI in exactly one well-grounded way: simulating other quantum systems — the electrons in a drug molecule, the atoms in a battery material — is something a quantum computer can do natively, while a classical computer has to painstakingly approximate it, and the approximation gets exponentially harder as the molecule grows. So instead of asking a quantum computer to "think faster," the real near-term idea is to use it as a data source: generate quantum-accurate training examples a classical computer never could, then train an ordinary AI model on that data. The other options here are real misconceptions — quantum computers are not general-purpose faster processors, exponential ML speedups from quantum linear algebra keep evaporating once you account for getting the data IN, and superposition doesn't let you store extra parameters for free; measuring it collapses everything back down to ordinary bits.
explain.y: The two AI-via-quantum routes that sound the most impressive on paper are also the shakiest in practice. Quantum optimization (QAOA, annealing) is a heuristic — no proven advantage over the best classical solvers for any practically useful problem class yet. Quantum linear-algebra speedups (HHL and its descendants) promise exponential gains for the matrix operations inside ML, but two things gut the naive version: the input has to be loaded into a quantum state first (the "data-loading toll"), and Tang's dequantization results (arXiv 1807.04271) show that once a classical algorithm gets comparable sampling access to the data, several of these "exponential" speedups collapse back to polynomial. The best-grounded route is different in kind: Hamiltonian simulation — modeling how a quantum system evolves — is provably efficient on a quantum computer and believed to be classically hard in general, so a quantum device can generate training data (e.g. molecular ground-state properties) that no classical simulation can match at scale. That's quantum feeding AI real data, not quantum making AI's existing math faster.
explain.r: The rigorous result here is Huang et al.'s proof of a provable quantum advantage for machine learning specifically when the training data itself is generated by a quantum process (arXiv 2011.01938, with the experimental follow-up 2112.00778) — a model trained on quantum-native data can provably beat any classical-data model on certain prediction tasks, in contrast to speedup claims for classical data, which remain unproven or actively disproven. Tang's dequantization program (arXiv 1807.04271) is the load-bearing counter-evidence against naive HHL-for-ML enthusiasm: several "exponential" quantum ML speedups reduce to polynomial once a classical algorithm is granted ℓ2-norm sampling access analogous to quantum state preparation. Aaronson's skeptical framing (Nature Physics 11, 291, 2015) predates both results and still holds up: the exponential dimension of Hilbert space is necessary but not sufficient for a real speedup, because reading the answer back out costs you the exponent right back. Ranked honestly: quantum-native training data (real, narrow, near-term) beats combinatorial-optimization heuristics (unproven), which beats a raw sampling advantage (fragile, easily dequantized), which beats a general linear-algebra speedup for ML (mostly oversold).

signal: Quantinuum, NVIDIA, and Pfizer combined a transformer model with reinforcement learning ("ADAPT-GQE") to generate molecular-simulation quantum circuits, cutting circuit-generation time by orders of magnitude versus the standard ADAPT-VQE method while matching its accuracy — demonstrated on the antidepressant imipramine and run on Quantinuum's Helios-1 hardware (arXiv 2607.22468, posted 2026-07-30; preprint, not yet peer-reviewed).
